justification: The article delivers exactly the angle CONTENT_PLAN.md §7.3 row 8 promises ('Counts explored nodes with vs without pruning'), and that angle is a genuine differentiator, confirmed by fetching the field directly. GeeksforGeeks's general backtracking-algorithms page (WebFetched) describes a 'choose-explore-backtrack' framework in the abstract and lists N-Queens/Sudoku/knight's-tour/rat-in-a-maze as examples but 'does not measure or count nodes explored with versus without pruning... no quantitative analysis of algorithm efficiency.' GfG's dedicated N-Queens backtracking page (also WebFetched) goes further than most tutorials -- it presents naive vs. two optimized (hashing-array, then bitmask) variants -- but still only states asymptotic O(n!) for all three; it 'does not count or measure actual nodes/calls explored. No concrete node-exploration metrics or comparative counts are included.' This article does exactly that gap-fill: SolveNaive/SolvePruned share the identical recursion shape and instrument every call with a counter, producing real, run numbers (2,057 vs. 109,601 nodes at n=8; a four-point scaling table from n=4 to n=10 showing the fraction shrink from 26% to 0.36%; 11 vs. 87,381 nodes on a 4x4 Sudoku board small enough to brute-force in full) -- most tutorials, this article's own closing section notes, 'just assert pruning helps without measuring it,' and the comparison pages bear that out. No filler: the opening paragraph goes straight into the N-Queens setup and defines 'state-space tree' at first use; the closing section ('What these numbers do and don't prove') is a substantive, specific claim about what the measurements do and do not establish (real counts at specific sizes vs. no evidence about growth past n=10 or about worst-case order), not a restated-headings summary or a feel-good conclusion paragraph. Headings are specific to content ('Choose, explore, un-choose', 'Eight queens, checked early versus checked late', 'The same pattern on a grid of digits: a Sudoku solver') with no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways heading anywhere, and checking three algorithms-pillar siblings (recursion.md, breadth-first-and-depth-first-search.md, dijkstra-shortest-path.md) confirms none share this article's heading pattern or phrasing -- each pillar article has its own distinct heading voice, so there is no templated, mass-produced feel across the pillar. Front matter is accurate and non-clickbait: title and description both state precisely what the article does (the choose/explore/un-choose template, N-Queens and Sudoku in C#, measuring how many nodes pruning skips) with no superlatives, no 'ultimate guide', no unearned promise. No NEEDS_MARKUS, TODO, lorem-ipsum, or other placeholder markers anywhere in the file (checked by pattern search). No ad code, ad placeholder, or analytics snippet of any kind. Sourcing: all three front-matter sources (Knuth's TAOCP Vol. 4 Fascicle 5, Sedgewick & Wayne's Algorithms 4th ed. §6.6, the C# language specification's array-creation section) are cited inline at the claim they support. The Knuth citation is handled correctly for an unopenable primary source: the article attributes only a general, well-known characterization of backtracking to Knuth ('search a state space depth-first, and whenever a partial choice cannot possibly extend to a solution, abandon that branch') without a page number and without presenting it as a direct quotation, which is exactly what the sourcing rule requires for a source the writer could not fully verify against a specific page. I fetched the cited C# language-specification page directly and confirmed §17.3 states verbatim 'Elements of arrays created by array_creation_expressions are always initialized to their default value ([§9.3])' -- the article's paraphrase ('the C# language specification guarantees that elements of an array created by new are always initialized to their type's default value') is accurate and is presented as a paraphrase, not a fabricated quotation. The Sedgewick & Wayne citation is used for the well-known, uncontroversial fact that exhaustive search blows up combinatorially, which is the kind of claim the brief permits attaching to a source without a page number. On the copying/close-paraphrase check: spot-checking distinctive sentences and the general backtracking description against the two GfG pages and Wikipedia's Backtracking article found no verbatim or near-verbatim overlap -- this article's 'choose, explore, un-choose' terminology and framing differs from GfG's 'choose-explore-backtrack' phrasing, and the running examples (N-Queens with explicit diagonal-tracking arrays, a generated-not-hand-typed Sudoku base grid, a deliberately small 4x4 Sudoku board sized for an exact naive-vs-pruned count) are the article's own, not reused from any comparison source's running example. Exercises are placed mid-article (not bunched under a single 'Exercises' heading) and vary in form (find-the-missing-check, does-fill-order-change-the-count); both keep their code and output strictly inside the collapsed :::solution::: block, so neither gives away the answer before the question. The diagram (Figure 1, a partial 4-queens state-space tree with one pruned branch) is deliberately scoped small and its caption states what to notice; it has title/desc for accessibility. No internal cross-links appear in the body (only external primary-source links), so the absence of a docs/crosslinks/algorithms/backtracking.md file is correct, not an omission. Why not higher: (1) this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before this review began, so the live phrase-level search pass the brief specifies for spot-checking distinctive sentences across the wider web could not be run; originality was instead verified by directly fetching and reading back the two most relevant GeeksforGeeks pages and Wikipedia's Backtracking article, which found no overlap and independently confirmed the article's core differentiator is absent from existing top results, but this is narrower coverage than a full-budget search pass would give. (2) The value-add, while genuine and well-executed, stays within a fairly narrow scope -- N-Queens and one small Sudoku board, one specific pruning technique (early constraint checking vs. late) -- rather than also measuring a second pruning strategy (e.g. constraint propagation/forward-checking) or a harder instance, so depth is comparable to rather than clearly exceeding the strongest possible treatment of this exact query.
